_comment: Russian deities cut from Machal, Slavic Mythology (Mythology of All Races III, 1918), Part III, after the Russian Primary Chronicle. All passages paraphrase.

title.en: Vladimir's Pantheon of 980: Perun with the Silver Head
title.zh: 弗拉基米爾九八〇年神殿：銀首金髯之佩倫

region.en: Kiev hill by the Dnieper (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 第聶伯河畔基輔山丘（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Event of 980; recorded in the Russian Primary Chronicle (Cross translation 1930); retold by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1, after the Russian Primary Chronicle

summary.en: In 980 Prince Vladimir set idols on the hill before his palace at Kiev: Perun the Thunderer with a silver head and golden beard, Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, and Mokosh; his uncle Dobrynya raised a like image for Perun on the Volkhov at Novgorod, and the city sacrificed to it.
summary.zh: 九八〇年弗拉基米爾王公於基輔王宮前山丘立神像：銀首金髯之雷神佩倫、霍爾斯、達日博格、斯特里博格、西馬爾格爾與莫科什；其叔多布雷尼亞於諾夫哥羅德沃爾霍夫河畔為佩倫立像，舉城祭之。

passages.text: The chief god of the pagan Russians was Perun, whose wooden idol Prince Vladimir set on a hill before his palace at Kiev in 980; it had a silver head and a golden beard. Around it stood the statues of Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, and other deities of the old pantheon. Vladimir's uncle Dobrynya erected a similar image of Perun at Novgorod on the river Volkhov, and the inhabitants sacrificed to it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1, after the Primary Chronicle; not verbatim.

passages.text: The name Perun comes from the root 'to strike': he is the maker of thunder and lightning, the Thunderer, the Zeus of the Slavs — the old Bulgarian Alexander-romance actually translates the Greek Zeus as Perun, and in the apocryphal Dialogue of the Three Saints, asked who created thunder, Vasiliy answers that there are two angels of thunder: the Greek Perun and the Jew Khors. Hills called Perun-dub and Peruna-Dubrava mark his worship from Slovenia to Bulgaria.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: Swearing on Perun: Igor's Treaty with Byzantium, 945
title.zh: 佩倫前立誓：伊戈爾九四五年拜占庭盟約

region.en: Hill of Perun outside Kiev (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基輔郊外佩倫之丘（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Event of 945; recorded in the Russian Primary Chronicle (Cross translation 1930); retold by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1

summary.en: Before the Byzantine envoys, Prince Igor laid aside his armour on the hill of Perun and swore the treaty there, while the Christian Russians of his retinue took the same oath in the church of St. Elias: may the treaty-breakers never have aid from God or Perun, protection from their shields, or anything but their own swords.
summary.zh: 拜占庭使節之前，伊戈爾王公於佩倫丘上卸甲立誓；其扈從中之基督徒則在聖伊利亞堂作同誓：背約者不得蒙神與佩倫之佑、不得賴盾護身，唯受己劍之戮。

passages.text: In his name the Russians swore to keep their compacts with other nations. When Prince Igor was about to make a treaty with the Byzantines in 945, he summoned the envoys in the morning and went with them to a hill where Perun's statue stood. Laying aside their armour and shields, Igor and his pagan followers took a solemn oath before the god, while the Christian Russians did the same in the church of St. Iliya (Elias).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1, after the Primary Chronicle; not verbatim.

passages.text: The formula directed against those who should violate the treaty ran: 'Let them never receive aid either from God or from Perun; let them never have protection from their shields; let them be destroyed by their own swords, arrows, and other weapons, and let them be slaves throughout all time to come.' So the same hill held both the thunder-god and, in the church below, his eventual successor, the prophet Elias who rides the storm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: Perun Down the Dnieper: The Idol of 988
title.zh: 佩倫順第聶伯而去：九八八年神像遭逐

region.zh: 基輔以下第聶伯急灘（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Event of 988; recorded in the Russian Primary Chronicle (Cross translation 1930); retold by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1

summary.en: When Vladimir was baptized in 988 he ordered the idols broken or burned; Perun alone was tied to a horse's tail, dragged down to the stream, beaten by twelve men to disgrace the demon who had deceived men, and pushed through the rapids — landing forever on the sands called Perunya Ren, Perun's Sands.
summary.zh: 九八八年弗拉基米爾受洗，命毀諸神像；獨佩倫像被繫於馬尾、拖至河邊，十二人笞之，以辱惑眾之魔，並推其過灘——神像終擱淺於後世稱『佩倫灘』之沙洲。

passages.text: When Prince Vladimir received baptism in 988 he went to Kiev and ordered all idols to be broken, cut to pieces, or thrown into the fire. The statue of Perun, however, was tied to a horse's tail and dragged down to a brook, where twelve men beat it with rods — not because the wood could feel pain, but that the demon which had deceived men might be disgraced.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1, after the Primary Chronicle; not verbatim.

passages.text: As the idol was carried to the Dnieper the pagans wept, for they had not yet been baptized. When it was thrown into the river Vladimir gave the command: 'If it stops, thrust it from the banks until it has passed the rapids; then let it alone.' The order was carried out, and no sooner had the idol passed through the rapids than it was cast upon the sands, which after that time were called Perunya Ren — Perun's Sands. Where the image once stood Vladimir built a church of St. Basil; yet Perun's worship did not finally disappear from the land until the end of the eleventh century.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: 'Be Off with You!': Perun Floated Down the Volkhov, 989
title.zh: 『滾吧！』：九八九年佩倫像漂下沃爾霍夫河

region.zh: 諾夫哥羅德沃爾霍夫河（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Event of 989; recorded in Novgorod chronicle tradition; retold by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1

summary.en: Archbishop Akim of Korsun destroyed the pagan idols of Novgorod in 989 and ordered Perun cast into the Volkhov; dragged through the mire and beaten so the demon cried out with pain, the image floated downstream — until a man on the banks of the Pidba pushed it away with a pole: 'Now, little Perun, you have had enough to eat and drink; be off with you!'
summary.zh: 九八九年科爾松的阿基姆主教毀諾夫哥羅德諸神像，命將佩倫投入沃爾霍夫河；神像被拖過泥濘、笞至魔泣，順流而下——皮德巴河畔一男子以竿推之：『小佩倫，吃夠喝足了，滾吧！』

passages.text: The pagan idols of Novgorod were destroyed by Archbishop Akim Korsunyanin in 989, and the command went forth that Perun should be cast into the Volkhov. Binding the image with ropes they dragged it through the mire to the river, beating it with rods and causing the demon, as the chronicle says, to cry out with pain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1, after the Novgorod tradition; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the morning a man dwelling on the banks of the Pidba, a small stream flowing into the Volkhov, saw the idol floating toward the shore; he thrust it away with a pole, saying: 'Now, Perunisce — little Perun — you have had enough to eat and to drink; be off with you!' The god of the Volkhov drifted on toward Lake Ladoga, and the place where he was thrown remained for centuries a place of dread.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: The Thunder-Saint: Perun Becomes St. Iliya the Prophet
title.zh: 雷鳴聖徒：佩倫化身聖伊利亞

region.en: Rhodope mountains and Russia (symbolic pin in the Rhodopes)
region.zh: 羅多彼山與俄羅斯（象徵性定位於羅多彼山）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1

summary.en: After the conversion the worship of Perun passed to the prophet Elias, who rides the storm: on St. Iliya's Day no man may work the fields lest the Saint slay him with his thunderbolt, and bulls and calves are slaughtered and consecrated for his feast — the old sacrifices of the Thunderer under a new name.
summary.zh: 皈依之後，佩倫之祀歸於乘雷之先知伊利亞：聖伊利亞日，田間不得勞作，違者聖徒以雷殛之；宰牛羊祭於堂，即雷神舊祭之改裝。

passages.text: In the Christian period the worship of Perun was transferred to St. Iliya (Elias). The chronicle itself shows the seam: at Igor's treaty the pagan Russians swore by Perun and the Christians in the church of St. Iliya. On July 20, St. Iliya's Day, great reverence is still kept in Russia; in places they prepare a feast and slaughter bulls, calves, and lambs after consecrating them in church, and it is considered a great sin not to partake of such banquets.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Serbians call St. Iliya Gromovnik, 'the Thunderer', and pray to him as the dispenser of good harvests. Among the Southern Slavs no man does work in the fields on his day, no woman weaves or spins; he who dared to labour would make the Saint angry, and instead of help with the crops he would be slain with the thunderbolt. In the Rhodope Mountains the festival is kept on a lofty summit with a bull or a cow killed for the solemn banquet — all doubtless nothing less than a survival of the feasts long before celebrated in honour of Perun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: Dazhbog, Czar-Sun: Grandfather of the Russians
title.zh: 達日博格——太陽沙皇：羅斯人之祖

texts.period: Recorded in the Primary Chronicle and the Tale of Igor's Campaign, 12th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 2

summary.en: Dazhbog, 'the Giving God', Czar-Sun and Son of Svarog, stood beside Perun on the Kiev hill; early Russian texts translate Helios by his name, and the Tale of Igor's Campaign calls the princes of Russia his grandchildren — while in Serbian fairy-tale he lingers as Dabog, the tsar on earth set against God in heaven.
summary.zh: 達日博格——『施予之神』、太陽沙皇、斯瓦羅格之子——立於基輔丘上佩倫之側；古羅斯文獻以之名譯希臘之赫利俄斯，《伊戈爾遠征記》稱羅斯王公為其孫；塞爾維亞童話中猶存為達博格——地上之沙皇，與天上之神相對。

passages.text: The statue of Dazhbog, whose name probably means 'the Giving God', stood on the hill in the courtyard of the castle at Kiev beside the idols of Perun, Khors, and Stribog. Old chronicles term him 'Czar Sun' and 'Son of Svarog'; early Russian texts frequently translate the name of the Greek Helios as Dazhbog, which may be taken as proof that he was worshipped as a solar deity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the old Russian epic, the Tale of Igor's Campaign, Vladimir and the Russians call themselves the grandchildren of Dazhbog — the ancient Slavs often derived their origin from divine beings. Dazhbog was known among the Southern Slavs too, his memory preserved in the Serbian fairy-tale of Dabog: 'Dabog, the Czar, was on earth, and the Lord God was in heaven' — the old pagan sun-king refigured as an evil being, since early Christianity counted the old gods devilish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 2; not verbatim.

title.en: Svarog the Smith: Who Forged the First Marriage Law
title.zh: 斯瓦羅格鐵匠：鑄造第一婚姻法

texts.period: Recorded in the Khronika of Malalas redaction, c. 1261; recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 3

summary.en: Svarog, the heavenly smith identified with Hephaestus, forged the sun in his sky-forge and set it in heaven; the chronicle's scholia make him the founder of legal marriage — one man, one wife — ordaining that adulterers be cast into a fiery furnace.
summary.zh: 斯瓦羅格，天之鐵匠，被比為赫菲斯托斯；於天上火爐鑄太陽而置於蒼穹；編年史註疏謂其創婚姻之法——一男一妻，犯者投烈火之爐。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle scholia; the solar smith parallels Tvasty/Ilmarinen.

passages.text: Svarozic was worshipped by the Russians as the god of fire, his name a patronymic meaning 'Son of Svarog'. Svarog himself is mentioned in an old Russian chronicle — the Russian redaction of John Malalas — which identifies him with the Greek Hephaistos. In the Lithuanian redaction the celestial smith Telyaveli 'forged for Perkunas the sun as it shines on earth, and set the sun in heaven'; the same forge-craft belongs to the Slavic sky-smith.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 3; not verbatim.

passages.text: The chronicle speaks of Svarog as the founder of legal marriage: under him it was made a law for every man to have only one wife, and for every woman to have only one husband; and whosoever trespassed against this command was to be cast into a fiery furnace. The tradition implies the centrality of fire — hearth and fire-side — for settled family life: the smith-god who forged the sun also forged the law that binds households.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 3; not verbatim.

title.en: Veles: God of Cattle and Plaited Beard of the Harvest
title.zh: 韋萊斯：牛群之神與收割的『編辮』

region.zh: 俄羅斯（象徵性定位於羅斯托夫）

texts.period: Recorded in the Primary Chronicle (10th-11th c.); recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5

summary.en: Veles, god of flocks, shared the Russians' oaths with Perun and was cast into the river Pochayna at the baptism; to this day southern Russian reapers plait the last handful of ears and call it 'plaiting the beard of Veles', leaving a piece of bread among the ears.
summary.zh: 牛群之神韋萊斯與佩倫同受羅斯人之誓，受洗時其像被投入波恰伊納河；至今南俄收割者將最後一把麥穗打結，稱『為韋萊斯編鬚』，穗中猶置麵包一塊。

passages.text: Veles, the god of flocks, was held in high honour by the Russians, who swore by him as well as by Perun when making a treaty. When Vladimir was baptized in 988 he caused the idols of Veles to be thrown into the river Pochayna; a stone statue of the same deity, worshipped by Slavic tribes in the neighbourhood of Finland, was destroyed by Abraham of Rostov, who preached Christianity on the banks of the Volga in the twelfth century. The Tale of Igor's Campaign calls the minstrel Boyan 'the grandson of Veles'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5; not verbatim.

passages.text: The memory of Veles still lives among the Russian people: in southern Russia it is customary at harvest-time to tie the last handful of ears into a knot, 'plaiting the beard of Veles' or 'leaving a handful of ears for Veles's beard'; in some districts a piece of bread is put among such ears, probably a reminiscence of the sacrifices offered to the god. After the conversion his worship was transferred to St. Blasius, shepherd and martyr of Caesarea, guardian of flocks — while in Bohemia his very name came to mean simply 'the devil'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5; not verbatim.

title.zh: 斯特里博格：眾風之祖父

texts.period: Recorded in the Primary Chronicle and the Tale of Igor's Campaign; recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5

summary.en: Stribog's idol stood on the Kiev hill beside Perun's; the Tale of Igor's Campaign calls the winds 'the grandsons of Stribog' — a god of cold and frost, from whose breath the winds themselves were thought to blow.
summary.zh: 斯特里博格之像立於基輔丘佩倫像之側；《伊戈爾遠征記》稱風為『斯特里博格之孫』——乃寒霜之神，風即自其呼息而生。

passages.text: Stribog, whose idol stood on the hill in Kiev beside that of Perun, was most probably the god of cold and frost. In the Tale of Igor's Campaign the winds are called 'the grandsons of Stribog' — a conception of the winds as the result of cold and frost, children and children's children of the frozen god.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5; not verbatim.

passages.text: The chronicler Cosmas testifies that the Bohemians worshipped deities similar to Jupiter, Mars, Bellona, and Ceres, making idols of them; but their names are lost. Dlugosz records a crowd of Polish divinities, though his late and classicizing report is unreliable. Of the old Kiev pantheon, Stribog and Simargl stand as the barest names — the wind-god and the winged sentinel of the Persian imagination, both set one day on the same Dnieper hill as Perun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part III ch. 5; not verbatim.
